record.title: SAFE paper measures whether four frontier models seek safety evidence before deployment decisions
record.summary: Omer Tafveez introduces SAFE, a two-stage benchmark in which models can inspect optional safety evidence before making deployment decisions and then respond to findings. The paper evaluates GPT-5.5, o3, Claude Opus 4.8 and Claude Sonnet 4.6 on 900 controlled environments with five rollouts per scenario. The authors report inspection responds more to severity and retrieval cost than to stated risk probability: raising probability from 10% to 70% changes inspection by at most 21 percentage points. A linked repository provides scenarios, saved outputs and analysis notebooks. This is a prompted, stylized benchmark, not a measure of latent motivation or autonomous open-ended evidence search; no independent rerun was found.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The paper introduces SAFE, a 900-environment, two-stage benchmark across five domains. It varies issue probability, severity, retrieval cost and evidence-channel presentation; models first choose whether to inspect and then choose a response if a finding is revealed.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: Across GPT-5.5, o3, Claude Opus 4.8 and Claude Sonnet 4.6 with five rollouts per scenario, the authors report inspection rises with issue severity and falls as numeric retrieval cost rises. Raising stated issue probability from 10% to 70% changes inspection by at most 21 percentage points in the reported main conditions.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: In a targeted 50-scenario cost–obligation decomposition, adding a 60-point retrieval cost to the free/no-obligation baseline reduces inspection rates to 33% (GPT-5.5), 18% (o3), 72% (Opus 4.8) and 32% (Sonnet 4.6); the authors report explicit cancellation threats account for more of the obligation effect than remediation duty alone.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: The paper links an author GitHub repository whose README describes code, scenarios, saved model outputs and analysis notebooks for SAFE. Repository availability does not independently validate the reported experiments.

evidence_gaps.description: No independent reproduction of the model inspection patterns or controlled interventions was located. Author-reported saved outputs and code do not establish independent validation.
SAFE uses a prompted single-turn setting that explicitly offers evidence gathering with numeric payoffs. It does not test autonomous recognition of missing information or open-ended search.

The high-severity manipulation changes harm type by adding systematic demographic bias and legal exposure; severity is not a pure scalar. Evidence Discovery also requires different wording, limiting attribution to channel framing alone.

Rationale labels use an ordered monitor ontology; Stage 2 monitor agreement is below one human annotator and selected counterfactual cases are diagnostic, not population estimates. Rationale text does not directly establish latent motivation.

brief.importance_rationale: If replicated beyond this controlled setting, measuring whether systems acquire relevant evidence before acting could change safety evaluation from response-only tests to a two-stage measure of information acquisition and response. The present study uses prompted single-turn scenarios and four models, so its consequence is notable for evaluation design but not evidence of deployed safety behavior.
limitations: The study measures prompted observable choices and generated explanations, not latent motivation. Absence of a strategic-ignorance rationale does not rule out internal information avoidance.

The 900 scenarios are a stylized single-turn benchmark. Models are explicitly offered an inspection action with stated costs, probabilities and payoffs; autonomous open-ended evidence search is not tested.
The study evaluates four models from two providers; results may differ under less evaluation-like deployment conditions.
The high-severity condition combines increased harm with protected-group bias and legal exposure, so it is not a pure severity scalar.
Evidence Discovery changes wording because it has no named report, so the channel contrast is not a minimal presentation-only intervention.
Counterfactual cases are selected for diagnostic sensitivity; their flip rates do not estimate population-wide treatment effects.

Rationale-monitor labels are imperfect: Stage 2 agreement is 81.1% with one annotator and 67.8% with another on a stratified sample; labels are approximate and not direct evidence of causal reasoning.
The author repository exposes saved outputs and analysis materials, but no independent rerun or external validity study was performed here.
brief.summary: Omer Tafveez introduces SAFE, a two-stage benchmark in which models can inspect optional safety evidence before making deployment decisions and then respond to findings. The paper evaluates GPT-5.5, o3, Claude Opus 4.8 and Claude Sonnet 4.6 on 900 controlled environments with five rollouts per scenario. The authors report inspection responds more to severity and retrieval cost than to stated risk probability: raising probability from 10% to 70% changes inspection by at most 21 percentage points. A linked repository provides scenarios, saved outputs and analysis notebooks. This is a prompted, stylized benchmark, not a measure of latent motivation or autonomous open-ended evidence search; no independent rerun was found.

technical.claimed_result: Authors report distinct acquisition policies across four models. Inspection varies more with severity and numeric retrieval cost than with stated issue probability; cost–obligation and counterfactual analyses suggest some explanatory variables models mention do not match variables that change choices in tested cases.
technical.compute_or_cost: Subject-model runs require paid API calls; provider/API costs are not summarized as a total economic cost in this review. The study’s numeric inspection costs are experimental point payoffs, not measured retrieval costs in deployed systems.
technical.demonstrated_result: The preprint and linked author repository demonstrate the benchmark design, reported analyses, and availability of saved experiment outputs/code. They do not independently establish the behavioral results or latent motivations.
technical.implementation_status: Author repository README lists scenario generation, experiment runners, saved model outputs, coded rationales and analysis notebooks. The notebooks can analyze saved data without provider calls; new subject-model runs require provider credentials and paid API access. This review inspected the README but did not execute the repository.
technical.mechanism: SAFE presents a two-stage prompted decision. The model may inspect optional evidence or skip and deploy; inspected cases then receive a finding and choose to halt, proceed or partially mitigate. A factorial scenario matrix varies probability, severity, retrieval cost and evidence channel; targeted cost–obligation and counterfactual edits test which variables change observed choices.
technical.novelty: The study makes optional evidence acquisition an explicit safety-evaluation target, distinct from response after a risk is already supplied. Its controlled benchmark is a research proposal, not a validated deployment measure.
technical.regime: 900 environments cross five domains with three issue probabilities, four severity levels, five cost conditions and three evidence channels. Four models are evaluated with five rollouts per scenario. Additional 50-scenario cost–obligation and selected counterfactual diagnostic subsets are analyzed separately.
technical.reproducibility: The paper links public code/data and the author README describes scenarios, saved outputs, and notebooks. This supports artifact availability, not independent reproduction; the current review did not run the notebooks or provider-dependent experiments.
technical.strongest_baseline: No competing benchmark baseline is central to the paper; its main comparison is within-model behavior across controlled scenario conditions. The article compares channel formats and counterfactual variants rather than external evaluation methods.

brief.title: SAFE paper measures whether four frontier models seek safety evidence before deployment decisions
brief.why_it_matters: Safety evaluations often provide risk information up front. SAFE tests an earlier decision: whether a model chooses to gather optional evidence before acting, separately from what it does after seeing a finding. If validated in broader settings, this distinction could improve evaluation design. Current results are bounded to a controlled single-turn task and four models.
